roof_form.rule: The gable, not the eave, is the composed and entered face.
roof_form.note: Inferred from massing_affinities rather than a literal roof_form statement in either node's text: german-fachwerk lists gable-front as 'canonical' ('the narrow taxed lot turns the gable to the square'); north-german-hall-house lists gable-front as 'common' and states 'the gable is the entrance and the only designed face.'

roof_pitch.rule: Steep — not less than about 45 degrees in either roofing material.

pitch.note: german-fachwerk.c04: roof pitch not less than 45 degrees for tile or slate, up to the 45-60 degree range stated in defining_characteristics. north-german-hall-house.c03: reed thatch at 45-50 degrees. The two ranges overlap at 45-50; the family range given here is the union.

gable_treatment.rule: The exposed frame carries through into the gable as the family's signature — jettied and jointed at the German street front, or the single composed elevation carrying the Grootdor at the hall house.

construction_type.rule: Load-bearing exposed timber frame (Fachwerk) with non-structural infill panels, not a masonry wall system.
construction_type.note: german-fachwerk is Fachwerk by definition. north-german-hall-house's own lineage entry states outright that it 'is built in Fachwerk and shares its jointing, its bay module and its infill practice entirely' with german-fachwerk (hybridizes_with, weight 0.5, inherits_kit: true) — the hall house is a plan/section type built in this framing system, not a different one.

primary_cladding.rule: Infill panels (Gefach) of wattle-and-daub or brick nogging between exposed structural timbers; the frame itself is never covered by applied siding.
primary_cladding.note: Explicit for german-fachwerk ('non-structural infill panels (Gefach) of wattle-and-daub or brick nogging'). Not independently restated for north-german-hall-house, whose own text describes the frame and the daub/thatch envelope but does not detail infill material — inferred via its direct, inherits_kit:true lineage to german-fachwerk.

foundation_expression.rule: The bottom sill sits clear of grade on a masonry or fired-brick plinth (Sockel); primary structural timber never touches the earth.

plinth_height.note: german-fachwerk.c02 states the plinth explicitly: at least 300 mm above finished grade. north-german-hall-house's own constraints (c01-c05) do not restate a plinth number; the practice is carried here on the strength of the shared framing system and general exposed-timber-frame vernacular practice, not on an explicit hall-house citation.

corner_quoin.rule: No masonry quoin of any kind — the corner is a structural timber post, exposed, not a masonry assembly.
corner_quoin.note: Both members expose the frame fully at the corner; there is no masonry corner treatment to speak of. See corner_board for the parallel finding on the frame trade's own side.

corner_board.rule: No applied corner board either — the structural corner post is exposed on the finished building, not concealed under trim.
corner_board.note: german-fachwerk's own diagnostic_tells state the frame is exposed 'never behind it'; a Fachwerk or hall-house corner covered by a board the way a clapboard building's is would misrepresent the type.

order.rule: No classical order or apparatus in either member. german-fachwerk's only classical contact is carved Renaissance-pattern-book ornament (rosettes, Vitruvian scroll, dentil bands) quoted onto the sill beam and brackets via a `references` edge with `inherits_kit: false` — vocabulary quoted onto the timber, not a real order, entablature or column system. north-german-hall-house has no classical reference of any kind.
